introduction: Xenophon, Cyropaedia 5.1.2–18 and 6.1.31–36. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

The core events follow Xenophon’s literary account of Cyrus the Great. Present and imperfect forms replace some original tense constructions. Panthea’s refusal and appeal remain central. The reflective questions are the course’s, not quotations.
Ask who acts and who is affected: a passive subject is not necessarily a person without agency.

reading.translation:
Panthea is a captive. Araspas is appointed her guardian by Cyrus. The woman was guarded by him. This Cyrus is not the Greeks’ ally in the Anabasis, but the earlier king.

Araspas trusts himself. He thinks he can master his desires. Cyrus does not trust himself in the same way and does not wish to see the beautiful woman.

Time passes, and Araspas desires the woman. He makes proposals to her. Panthea is not persuaded; she loves her husband and does not accept the wrongdoing.

The woman is frightened by her guardian’s threats. Araspas says he will use force. Panthea does not remain silent; she sends a messenger to Cyrus and seeks help.

Cyrus sends Artabazus. Araspas is rebuked by Artabazus. For the guardian ought to have protected the woman, not frightened her. Now he himself is ashamed.

Consider the two voices: “The guardian frightens the woman” and “The woman is frightened by the guardian.” The same person does wrong. The woman’s suffering does not become invisible because of the grammatical voice.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — φυλάττω: protection and custody

blocks.title: φυλάττω: protection and custody
body: φυλάττω can mean guard, watch, or protect. The English choice matters: guarding someone can provide security, restrict freedom, or both. Context supplies the relationship.

ὁ φύλαξ names a guard; φυλάττεται can mean “is guarded.” Ask who holds power and whose interests the guarding serves. The word family helps trace actions without deciding their moral quality in advance.

sections.title: 1. Present passive: who receives the action?
body: A passive verb makes the affected person or thing the grammatical subject. Compare ὁ φύλαξ φυλάττει τὴν γυναῖκα, “the guard protects the woman,” with ἡ γυνὴ φυλάττεται, “the woman is protected.” Present passive forms use the same endings as the present middle.
The endings are -ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -ονται. A form alone does not prove a passive meaning; read the verb’s meaning and the surrounding sentence.

sections.title: 2. Imperfect passive: action in progress
body: The imperfect passive uses augment, present stem, and middle/passive secondary endings. ἐφυλάττετο means “she was being protected” in the appropriate context. The imperfect can describe an ongoing state of custody without implying a completed rescue.
Compare present φυλάττεται and imperfect ἐφυλάττετο. Both can be passive; tense and aspect are separate from voice. Remember first singular -όμην and third plural -οντο.

sections.title: 3. Agent, instrument, and responsibility
body: A personal agent is commonly expressed by ὑπό plus genitive: ὑπὸ τοῦ φύλακος, “by the guard.” An instrument can be a bare dative: λίθῳ, “with a stone.” Keep these roles distinct from the person affected.

A passive can leave the agent unstated. That is a grammatical choice, not evidence that nobody acted. In an ethical reading, ask whether the sentence names, obscures, or leaves open the person responsible.

sections.title: 4. Active, middle, passive, and deponent
body: Active, middle, and passive describe different relationships between a subject and an action. A middle may involve the subject’s own interest, as in choosing for oneself; a passive presents the subject as affected. Deponent verbs use middle forms with meanings such as “answer” or “wish.”

Do not translate mechanically with “is being” whenever you see -ται. βούλεται means “wishes,” αἱρεῖται “chooses” in a suitable context, and φυλάττεται may be middle or passive depending on the sentence.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Cyropaedia
body: The Cyropaedia, often translated “Education of Cyrus,” is an extended literary exploration of Cyrus the Great’s formation and leadership. It blends narrative, political reflection, and exemplary characterization. It is not a straightforward documentary biography of Persian institutions.

Its eight books follow Cyrus the Great from education to conquest, imperial organization, and death. This Cyrus is the sixth-century founder of Persian power, not Cyrus the Younger of the Anabasis. The opening question is striking: why do people so often resist rulers, and how could Cyrus secure obedience across so many peoples? Childhood training becomes the starting point for a much larger inquiry into power.

Xenophon combines campaigns, speeches, friendships, rivalries, and domestic stories to explore leadership. Rewards and persuasion stand beside military force; admiration for the ruler sits beside questions about dependence on him. The final account of decline after Cyrus complicates an uncomplicated success story. Read this as a crafted political and educational narrative, not a reliable transcript of sixth-century Persian court life.

Reading invitation: compare the opening discussion of obedience in Book 1 with Araspas’s confidence about desire in Book 5 and its consequences in Book 6. Panthea’s story makes the problem personal: can someone entrusted with power govern himself? Then glance at the close of Book 8. What can a leader build that will survive him? The whole-work link opens Henry Graham Dakyns’s English translation, revised by F. M. Stawell.

Our reading follows Araspas and Panthea in 5.1 and 6.1. Araspas initially claims confidence in his power to control desire; later his conduct exposes the weakness of that claim. The adaptation compresses separated scenes and uses passive constructions to track custody and agency.

sections.title: Panthea is a person, not a test object
body: Panthea’s position as a captive creates an unequal relationship with the man entrusted with guarding her. Her refusal and appeal for protection matter. Araspas’s responsibility does not pass to her because he experiences desire.

Read the scene twice: first follow Araspas’s claims about himself; then follow Panthea’s choices within her constraints. What information becomes visible in the second reading? A lesson about self-mastery must also attend to the person exposed to another’s power.

sections.title: The passive can reveal or hide an actor
body: “She is guarded” puts Panthea at the center of the sentence, but it can leave the guard unnamed. “She is guarded by Araspas” supplies the agent. Neither version by itself tells us whether that guard is trustworthy.

Try rewriting a sentence about custody in active and passive forms. Keep the event the same, then explain which person each version foregrounds. Grammar changes emphasis; it does not erase responsibility.

sections.title: A confidence claim meets conduct
body: Compare “I can control myself” with evidence of how someone acts when another person refuses. The story’s tension comes from the gap between confident speech and later behavior.

The banner imagines a guarded setting and a message, not a documented Persian interior. Finish by naming one limit of this literary evidence and one question about responsibility that it helps you ask. Avoid treating the captive’s vulnerability as a moral defect.

questions.prompt: Choose the normal personal-agent construction here.

choices.feedback: Reconsider: ὑπό plus genitive. A personal agent is commonly expressed by ὑπό plus genitive: ὑπὸ τοῦ φύλακος, “by the guard.” An instrument can be a bare dative: λίθῳ, “with a stone.” Keep these roles distinct from the person affected. A passive can leave the agent unstated. That is a grammatical choice, not evidence that nobody acted.
